issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme permitting executive officers to take over a proprietor’s property on an unreviewable determination that the proprietor habitually infringed tenants’ rights abridges the constitutional right to property.
material_facts: The petitioner held an estate and had the right to manage it and enjoy possession of it.
The Court of Wards took possession and assumed superintendence of the estate under the challenged statutory scheme.
The scheme supplied no procedure for determining whether a proprietor habitually infringed tenants’ rights, and the relevant executive discretion could not be challenged in a civil court.
The petitioner’s possession and management were suspended for an indefinite period, and the sums allowed for his expenses were left to the Court of Wards’ discretion.
issues.conclusion: The scheme infringed the petitioner’s property right under article 19(1)(f) and was void to that extent; possession was to be restored to him.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property. Sections 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, and 6, 7 and 27 of the Ajmer Government Wards Regulation, 1888, operated to permit an executive takeover based on subjective determination without a means to challenge that determination in a civil court. The Court held that this abridged the protected property right. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: constitutional_property_right_challenge and executive_property_takeover and unreviewable_executive_determination and indefinite_loss_of_possession_or_management

predicates.constitutional_property_right_challenge: The proceeding challenges state action as an infringement of a constitutional property right.
predicates.executive_property_takeover: Executive officers took possession of or assumed management of a proprietor’s property.
predicates.unreviewable_executive_determination: The executive decision depended on its own determination, with no available civil-court review of that determination.
predicates.indefinite_loss_of_possession_or_managem: The proprietor’s possession or management was suspended for an indefinite period.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property-right challenge concerns an executive takeover based on an unreviewable determination that causes indefinite loss of possession or management, the takeover infringes the property right.

issues.legal_issue: A punitive deprivation of property resting on executive discretion and lacking an opportunity for judicial review is not a reasonable restriction on the constitutional property right.
material_facts: The statutory scheme was intended to punish proprietors who habitually infringed tenants’ rights by placing their property under the Court of Wards’ superintendence.
The takeover could deprive a proprietor of possession for an indefinite period on the subjective determination of executive officers.
The proprietor had no right to have the correctness of that determination tested in a civil court.
issues.conclusion: The challenged measure was not a reasonable restriction within article 19(5) and could not be sustained on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions on the right protected by article 19(1)(f). The Court held that a punitive measure which makes enjoyment of the right depend on executive discretion and denies recourse to a civil court completely negates the right and cannot be regarded as reasonable. It considered section 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, together with sections 6, 7 and 27 of the Ajmer Government Wards Regulation, 1888. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: constitutional_property_right_challenge and punitive_property_deprivation and executive_discretion_controls_deprivation and no_civil_court_review

predicates.constitutional_property_right_challenge: The proceeding challenges state action as an infringement of a constitutional property right.
predicates.punitive_property_deprivation: The state measure deprives a proprietor of possession or management as punishment for the proprietor’s conduct.
predicates.executive_discretion_controls_deprivatio: Executive officers’ discretion determines whether the deprivation occurs or continues.
predicates.no_civil_court_review: The proprietor cannot obtain civil-court review of the executive determination.

issues.definition: A punitive deprivation is not a reasonable restriction when executive discretion controls it and the affected proprietor cannot seek civil-court review in a constitutional property-right challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A law that suspends a proprietor’s management of an estate without acquiring or extinguishing proprietary rights is outside the constitutional saving for laws concerning acquisition, extinguishment or modification of such rights.
material_facts: The challenged measure permitted the Court of Wards to assume superintendence of a proprietor’s property because of habitual infringement of tenants’ rights.
The measure suspended the proprietor’s possession and management but did not acquire the estate for the State or extinguish the proprietor’s ownership.
The suspension of management could continue for a definite or indefinite period.
issues.conclusion: The challenged law was not saved by article 31-A because a suspension of management was not an acquisition, extinguishment or modification of proprietary rights within that article.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects qualifying laws providing for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or for extinguishment or modification of such rights. The Court interpreted “modification” in that context as a change to the proprietary right, comparable to its extinguishment, and held that a mere suspension of management for a time did not qualify. It considered section 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and law_suspends_management and ownership_remains_with_proprietor and no_state_acquisition_of_estate_or_rights

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a law under constitutional property protections.
predicates.law_suspends_management: The law suspends the proprietor’s management of the property for a period.
predicates.ownership_remains_with_proprietor: The proprietor retains ownership of the property despite the suspension of management.
predicates.no_state_acquisition_of_estate_or_rights: The law does not provide for the State to acquire the estate or rights in it.

issues.definition: In a constitutional validity challenge, a law that suspends management while leaving ownership with the proprietor and providing for no State acquisition is outside the property-acquisition saving.
